#!/usr/bin/env bash
# PreToolUse guard for the PRD -> WinGet configuration workflow.
#
# Keeps the work inside the winget-config-maintainer agent, which sets its
# own model and effort:
#   1. The prd-to-winget-config skill can't run through the Skill tool.
#      The agent has it preloaded, so it never needs the tool.
#   2. Calls to any project agent can't override a model or effort that
#      its definition sets.
#   3. Only the agent edits .config/configuration.winget.
#   4. The agent leaves PRD.md alone, since that file is the user's.
#
# Exit code 2 blocks the tool call and shows Claude the message on stderr.
# It covers Claude's file tools, not shell commands that write files.

agent="winget-config-maintainer"
skill="prd-to-winget-config"

if ! command -v jq >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "guard-winget-config: jq isn't installed, so the guard is off." >&2
  exit 1
fi

input=$(cat)
get() { jq -r "$1 // empty" <<<"$input" 2>/dev/null; }
block() {
  echo "$1" >&2
  exit 2
}
# True when the project agent named $1 sets model or effort in its frontmatter.
pins() {
  local file
  [[ -n $1 ]] || return 1
  file=$(grep -lxF "name: $1" "${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR:-$(get '.cwd')}"/.claude/agents/*.md 2>/dev/null | head -n 1)
  [[ -n $file ]] && sed -n '2,/^---$/p' "$file" | grep -qE '^(model|effort):'
}

shopt -s nocasematch # Windows and macOS paths ignore case
tool=$(get '.tool_name')
caller=$(get '.agent_type')

case "$tool" in
  Skill)
    name=$(get '.tool_input.skill')
    if [[ "$name" == "$skill" || "$name" == *":$skill" ]]; then
      block "The $skill skill runs only inside the $agent agent, which loads it at startup. Delegate the task to that agent."
    fi
    ;;
  Agent | Task)
    target=$(get '.tool_input.subagent_type')
    if [[ -n "$(get '.tool_input.model')$(get '.tool_input.effort')" ]] && pins "$target"; then
      block "The $target agent sets its own model and effort. Call it again without the model and effort parameters."
    fi
    ;;
  Write | Edit | MultiEdit | NotebookEdit)
    path=$(get '.tool_input.file_path // .tool_input.notebook_path')
    path=${path//\\//} # Windows separators
    case "$path" in
      */.config/configuration.winget | .config/configuration.winget)
        if [[ "$caller" != "$agent" ]]; then
          block "Only the $agent agent edits .config/configuration.winget. Delegate the change to that agent, after updating PRD.md if the requirements changed."
        fi
        ;;
      */PRD.md | PRD.md)
        if [[ "$caller" == "$agent" ]]; then
          block "PRD.md is the user's file. Leave it unchanged and put the change you'd suggest in your report."
        fi
        ;;
    esac
    ;;
esac

exit 0

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Stop hook: after each turn, saves this session's transcripts to the orphan
# branch agent-transcripts and pushes it, for the meta-reviewer agent:
#   transcripts/<session-id>.jsonl            the session transcript
#   transcripts/<session-id>/subagents/...    its subagents' transcripts
#
# The work happens in a sparse git worktree inside .git, so the working
# branch, its index and its files stay untouched. Runs are idempotent: an
# unchanged transcript makes no commit, and an up-to-date branch no push.
# The hook returns at once and works in the background. It never reports
# failure; the last run's log is .git/agent-transcripts.log.

branch=agent-transcripts

# Hand the hook input to a detached copy of this script, then return.
if [[ $1 != --worker ]]; then
  input=$(cat)
  launcher="nohup"
  command -v setsid >/dev/null 2>&1 && launcher=setsid
  "$launcher" bash "$0" --worker <<<"$input" >/dev/null 2>&1 &
  exit 0
fi

input=$(cat)
command -v jq >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 0
field() { jq -r ".$1 // empty" <<<"$input" 2>/dev/null; }
session=$(field session_id)
session=${session//[^A-Za-z0-9._-]/_} # safe as a file name
transcript=$(field transcript_path)
repo=${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR:-$(field cwd)}
[[ -n $session && -f $transcript ]] || exit 0
gitdir=$(git -C "$repo" rev-parse --path-format=absolute --git-common-dir 2>/dev/null) || exit 0
exec >"$gitdir/agent-transcripts.log" 2>&1
set -x

# One run at a time; a lock older than 10 minutes is from a run that died.
lock="$gitdir/agent-transcripts.lock"
locked=false
for _ in {1..60}; do
  if mkdir "$lock" 2>/dev/null; then
    locked=true
    break
  fi
  find "$lock" -maxdepth 0 -mmin +10 -exec rmdir {} + 2>/dev/null
  sleep 2
done
$locked || exit 0
trap 'rmdir "$lock"' EXIT

export GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0 GIT_SSH_COMMAND=${GIT_SSH_COMMAND:-"ssh -o BatchMode=yes"}
worktree="$gitdir/agent-transcripts-worktree"
remote_ref="refs/remotes/origin/$branch"
# Sparse checkout is switched on per command, so the repo's config never changes.
wt() { git -C "$worktree" -c commit.gpgsign=false -c core.sparseCheckout=true -c core.sparseCheckoutCone=false "$@"; }
fetch() { git -C "$repo" fetch -q --no-tags origin "+refs/heads/$branch:$remote_ref"; }
has_remote() { git -C "$repo" show-ref -q --verify "$remote_ref"; }

fetch
if [[ ! -e $worktree/.git ]]; then
  rm -rf "$worktree"
  git -C "$repo" worktree prune # drop the registration of a deleted worktree
  if git -C "$repo" show-ref -q --verify "refs/heads/$branch"; then
    git -C "$repo" worktree add -q --no-checkout "$worktree" "$branch"
  elif has_remote; then
    git -C "$repo" worktree add -q --no-checkout -b "$branch" "$worktree" "origin/$branch"
  else
    git -C "$repo" worktree add -q --orphan -b "$branch" "$worktree"
  fi || exit 0
fi

# Check out only this session's files; the branch holds every session's.
patterns=$(wt rev-parse --path-format=absolute --git-path info/sparse-checkout) || exit 0
mkdir -p "${patterns%/*}" && printf '%s\n' "/transcripts/$session.jsonl" "/transcripts/$session/" >"$patterns"

# Clear what a crashed run left behind, then build on the remote tip.
wt rebase --abort 2>/dev/null
if wt rev-parse -q --verify HEAD >/dev/null; then
  wt reset -q --hard
  if has_remote; then
    wt rebase -q -X theirs "origin/$branch" || {
      wt rebase --abort
      wt reset -q --hard "origin/$branch"
    }
  fi
elif has_remote; then
  wt checkout -q -B "$branch" "origin/$branch"
fi

copy() { mkdir -p "${2%/*}" && { cmp -s "$1" "$2" || cp "$1" "$2"; }; }
copy "$transcript" "$worktree/transcripts/$session.jsonl"
# Subagent transcripts can sit in nested folders, so walk the whole tree.
subagents=${transcript%.jsonl}/subagents
if [[ -d $subagents ]]; then
  while IFS= read -r -d '' file; do
    copy "$file" "$worktree/transcripts/$session/subagents/${file#"$subagents"/}"
  done < <(find "$subagents" -type f \( -name '*.jsonl' -o -name '*.meta.json' \) -print0)
fi

wt add -- "transcripts/$session.jsonl"
[[ -d $worktree/transcripts/$session ]] && wt add -A -- "transcripts/$session"
if ! wt diff --cached --quiet; then
  identity=()
  [[ -n $(wt config user.email) ]] ||
    identity=(-c user.name="agent-transcripts hook" -c user.email="agent-transcripts@localhost")
  wt "${identity[@]}" commit -q --no-verify -m "Save transcripts for session $session"
fi

# Push; if another session pushed first, replay on top and try again.
for _ in 1 2 3; do
  [[ $(wt rev-parse -q --verify HEAD) == "$(wt rev-parse -q --verify "origin/$branch")" ]] && break
  wt push -q --no-verify origin "HEAD:refs/heads/$branch" && break
  if ! { fetch && wt rebase -q -X theirs "origin/$branch"; }; then
    wt rebase --abort
    break
  fi
done
exit 0

# PRD: Windows 11 PC setup

Requirements for my Windows 11 PC, used mainly for software development and gaming, and to a lesser extent for office work. The winget-config-maintainer agent turns them into the WinGet configuration `.config/configuration.winget`.

## A living file, not a one-time setup

This PRD isn't single-use. I'll keep updating it as I add apps or change the PC, and after each change the agent updates the config and I rerun it on the same, already set-up PC.

Deleting a requirement doesn't undo it on the PC; to remove an app, list it under [Apps to remove](#apps-to-remove).

## How to read this

- Every requirement starts with an ID: **RUN** for how reruns behave, **SYS** for Windows itself, **APP** for apps, **SET** for look and feel.

## Reruns

## System

- **SYS-01** Windows 11 only: stop if the PC runs anything older
- **SYS-02** Developer Mode on
- **SYS-03** Long file paths (over 260 characters) allowed
- **SYS-04** Never sleep when plugged in; the screen still turns off when idle, on the Windows default timer

### Development

### Chat and calls

I agree with your point on naming apps versus naming the solution. The requirements should never specify or prescribe the tech stack of the solution. That's what I meant. Can you edit the GitHub issue with that correction? Regarding your second point, the owner of the workflow is up in the air at the moment. Can you just list it as out of scope for the issue? That sub-agent should be a background agent because I want this conversation to continue and we need to be doing other work in the meantime.

So for now, can you draft me the wording for a GitHub sub-issue just for the first sub-issue, which is the README and contributing markdown files?
Can you explain the point in the draft issue about using generic examples only? I don't understand why that bullet point is there.
I'm happy for there to be generic examples, but make them actually generic and not ones which are plausible for the specific repo. So any examples in that file should use analogies that are explicitly unrelated to this repo and can't be interpreted or misinterpreted as direction or presupposing an answer. So my example of the contract MD being analogous to a .pyi file for the contract of a Python library, that would be an example of a good generic example.
Using a background subagent, can you create a very thin claude.md file for the repository where the claude.md file merely points to the contributing.md file? Saying that if you're contributing to the repository, read that file first.

I'm just looking at the reviewer subagent outcomes and findings. I don't want all of these to be actioned, but some of them I do want actioned. Action the fix 4.2. For 4.3, I want it to be listed as out of scope, but subject to future work. Which relates to also fixing 0.4. Ignore 0.5. I believe 0.6 has already been addressed with my instruction around using only generic examples in contributing.md. I don't understand 0.7. Can you explain that a bit more before I make a decision on it? I don't understand 0.8. Can you explain it a bit more before I make a decision? Action a fix for 0.9. For 0.10, I want the winget facts to be disregarded, since I assume future agents will pick that up later on. For 0.11, I want that fixed, but I want that fixed just by adding a very minimalist comment to issue 2. Don't edit the issue, just add a comment. Fix 0.12 by adding an additional audit trail link for the transcript for this conversation to issue number 2.
Yes, please fix finding 7. Regarding finding 8, you're saying this morning's rule is that a requirement may name what ends up on the PC. I don't remember us agreeing to that. Can you flesh that out a bit more, what your understanding is of something I said earlier? I think we're not quite on the same page regarding that. To be clear, the requirement shouldn't specify a specific tech stack for the solution. Chrome is installed is not a thing that I foresee being included in the requirements. Does this make sense? And if so, is finding 8 still an actual issue?
Okay, I'm looking to wrap up this conversation and move on. At the start of this conversation, I said to check with me before actually making changes, and we worked on some drafts. So can you let me know if there's anything from this conversation which needs to be wrapped up before I close out this conversation? For example, are there any changes to issues or any commits to the repo which need to be pushed? Just list out the items that we need to wrap up in this conversation before I close it up.
Yeah, delete the local Claude.md file. Do point one of the things you need to wrap up, that being remove your Chrome sentence. Regarding point two of your wrap up, which references finding one, I want that to be listed in issue two as out of scope, but in need of future work. To be clear, it's out of scope for issue two, but it definitely needs to be done in the future.

===== c4ada59b-4ed6-5f7d-b07e-aeb1f41bd54f =====
I'm starting this chat in order to collaboratively work through issue 3 of the repo. To start, can you just read issue 3 from GitHub and also familiarize yourself with the repo before we begin?
Can you remove the second bullet point from the contributing.md section of issue 3? I don't want the contributing.md file to dictate how a contributor needs to interact with their own agent. The point of the contributing.md file is to detail information required for the agent to interact with the repository, not for how the human being interacts with the agent.
Thank you. Yes, I'd like a line recording this principle so a later session is aware that that is the purpose of the contributing.md file. So to restate, contributing.md file is intended to assist with how agents interact with the repository when contributing to the repository. It is not about how humans should interact with agents, and I want that recorded in issue 3, GitHub issue 3, as a comment to clarify for future work done to close out that issue. How I interact with agents shouldn't be recorded in contributing.md. It also shouldn't be recorded in issue 3 or any GitHub issue for now.
Agreed. Please trim them as you describe.
Okay, so how I want this conversation to go, starting with the contributing.md file, I'm going to ramble a bit about what I believe the contributing.md file should contain. I then want you to add any additional points as a GitHub comment in issue 3. That is, any points that I make in my ramble beyond what is already written in issue 2 and issue 3.
As I stated earlier, the purpose of a contributing.md file is to give the instructions for how a agent should interact with the repository when making contributions to the repository. It should state all the major files, such as the contract.md file and requirements.md file, and the purpose of each of those files. The purpose of the contributing.md file should be at the top of the contributing.md file itself.
Can you remove that note from the GitHub issue? I never agreed for there to be a note in the contributing.md file. Don't put a note in there.
[Request interrupted by user]
I also want the contributing.md file to document the delineation of who owns what is owned by the agent, what's owned by the human, and what's built collaboratively with joint ownership.
All good, I'll start a new chat now to continue the work in a separate agent session.

===== c934bbec-2feb-506c-a920-1441999d4807 =====
I want some work done on this repository, specifically the product requirements document markdown file, pod.md. Can you start just by reading that and getting yourself familiar with it?
Okay, I'm just going to speak while I'm reading the document, and I'll just give feedback and ramble a bit as I read through it. And then from that, I was hoping you could just repeat back to me what changes you understand based on my ramble, and we can go back and forth. So don't make any edits based on what I'm rambling at the moment, just try and digest my ramble and give it back to me in chat so we can agree upon what actually needs to be changed. So overall, my philosophy for this prd.md file is that it's meant to be purely about requirements, not about the solution. So this product requirements document file shouldn't presuppose or mention WinGet or WinGet configuration. I agree it should list the apps to install, the apps to remove. Actually, no. Even that's a bit too much. I think there needs to be a hierarchy of requirements where each level of requirements is used to derive the next level of requirements, and then the base level of requirements at the very bottom that then is used to decide upon the solution, which in all likelihood will involve WinGet, but that shouldn't come from me. That should be agent decided based on the requirements. So all these requirements, they should come from me, the human, potentially in collaboration with the agent. Certainly the highest level requirement should come 100% from me, the human. And then me as the human will try and derive the next level of requirements that are derived from the highest level requirement. And that process, I'm happy to do that in collaboration with an agent in chat, where ultimately me, the human, decides what goes into the requirements and needs to understand those requirements. So on and so forth for all the levels of requirements, each one being derived from the higher level. And then the very lowest level, the actual implementation, that should be 100% created by the agent, and me, the human, doesn't need to understand it. However, there needs to be a mechanism by which I can steer it, so I don't make any edits to the actual implementation. But there should be a markdown file, which is towards implementation steering. In that document, I can ask the agent to consider WinGet, but ultimately it's up to the AI agent to decide based on the steering and the requirements what the best implementation should be. And that could be agreeing with or not agreeing with the suggestions in the steering document. If there is a better way to go and fulfill the requirements. Another thing which should come out of the base requirements and are a even lower level than the lowest level requirement is the contract. So that should be decided upon similar to requirements in that it's a requirement that the interface or the contract needs to be a certain way, and I want to be able to understand that as the human. So I know that this isn't a Python library, but if it was the Python library, then it would be something like the signature of all the public Python functions and classes and methods, etc. For this, it'll probably be something like the way that this setup is run. So I might specify the contract as a setup.ps1 PowerShell executable file. That's just a suggestion. I'm not deciding that now, but that's the kind of thing I mean when I say that there needs to be an agreed contract. Can you just repeat that back to me in a structured way so that I can make sure we're on the same page? Don't actually try and implement any of this. Don't actually try and look deeper in deciding what the highest level requirement is or anything like that. we'll start the process of capturing those requirements after I've made sure that you've understood me correctly.
I think you've understood me correctly, but I'd like to make some adjustments. So I'd like to make an adjustment around steering and ignoring the steering. So I want the steering to be a steering.md file, as you suggested. And I want that file to have the format of a bullet point list. A bullet point list always starts with a keyword that is all caps. The keywords are always, never, favor, disfavor, consider. What I was mentioning before about considering WinGet, that would be a consider dot point. That can be ignored. The favor and disfavor points can also be ignored with justification. The always and never bullet points need to be met by the implementation. The difference between steering and the requirements is that the requirements are in the problem space, and this steering is about the solution space. Okay, going on to other things. Yes, I agree about tracing. Each requirement names the ID or the requirement above it that it comes from. So every line traces back to the top. I want to rename prd.md as requirements.md. Don't make any changes yet. Just reply so that I know you've understood me.
Answering your two checks, point one, you're correct. When the agent ignores a consider, it doesn't need a justification. Consider is just there for inspiration. It's not a preference. Around the second check, that is regarding when always or never conflicts with a requirement. Yes, the agent should stop. However, the always and never bullet points should never conflict with a requirement because they're in two different spaces. The requirements are in the problem space. And the steering is in the solution space. So the always or never bullet points in the steering file should be about things which should always or never be done in the implementation. Now, it might be the case that the always and never constraints in the steering file that constrain the implementation might mean that it's impossible to implement a solution that meets the requirements. That can be the case. But still, there shouldn't be a direct logical contradiction between the always and never bullet points in the steering document and the requirements because they operate in two different spaces. I want the clear delineation between the solution space and problem space to be included in the philosophy for how I want this system to work.
Okay, you got two additional checks. Point one, the contract sits on the boundary between the two spaces. I see what you mean. The steering can't conflict with the contract. I think it'd be better if the contract is spun off as its own separate document, contract.md. Regarding your second point, yes, I agree. The philosophy should live in the readme.md. Actually, no, it shouldn't live in the readme.md. It should be in the contributing.md file. I forget what the canonical word for that file is. It's either contributing.md or contributor.md or something like that. That contributing.md file should be referenced in the README file. To make sure I can confirm that you've understood, can you give me a mermaid diagram that shows all the different files or concepts within those files and relationships between these different artifacts? So the connectors in the mermaid diagram should give the relationship between these artifacts.
The assumption is incorrect. Using the deep modules principle, the contract should be narrow, and the requirements that it fulfills should be deep. So the mapping between the contract and the base requirements would be very noisy, because you'd have many, many, many base requirements mapping onto different elements of the contract. I also want to revise a part of this philosophy. The contract should be coming from the requirements as a whole, not from the base level requirements. That's because the requirements are not merely different levels of abstraction for the requirements. In other words, the base level shouldn't completely and holistically capture all the requirements. Some requirements can be stated in the middle levels completely sufficiently. It's only some requirements in the middle level that will lead to other derived requirements that give more detail, where lower level requirements are derived from higher level requirements, if that makes sense. As an example, the run requirement that currently exists, that would likely appear in one of the middle levels alongside apps to install, apps to remove, and look and feel. Those are all middle level requirements. However, the apps to install, apps to remove, look and feel, those would have some derived requirements at a lower level, whereas the run requirement may not need to be broken down into lower level requirements that are derived from or satisfy the high level run requirement, because run requirement is sufficient at that level of abstraction. Given this is how I want the requirements to work, the contract doesn't come from the base level, it comes from the requirements as a whole. All requirements at all levels need to be used to derive the appropriate contract.
Awesome, looks good. I'd like to make a note that a mermaid diagram similar to the one you provided me should be included in the contributing.md file. Not the exact one that you shared with me, since that one seems catered towards this conversation and isn't written in a way that you would expect from a file in a repo. You use second person in the diagram. Which you wouldn't expect from files in a repo. I'd also like the mermaid diagram in the contributing.md file to use color coding in order to distinguish between the artifacts that are ...100% owned by the agent, 100% owned by the human, or artifacts that are created collaboratively with shared ownership.
Yes, the README and contributing Markdown files are both shared ownership between the agent and the human. Awesome, thanks for creating the agreed changes Markdown file. Similar to that, can you give me a file that comprehensively summarizes where we've landed in the format of a GitHub issue? For now, I just want this one GitHub issue that summarizes where we've landed so that I can start a fresh agent session later on and pass that GitHub issue. Don't save the GitHub issue to GitHub yet. I just want you to create the draft file so that I can have a look at it and make sure that nothing was missed. I'll break up that GitHub issue later on into sub-issues, where each sub-issue is a piece of work that I complete collaboratively with an agent, similar to this conversation where I'm speaking and going back and forth with an agent. But don't break down that GitHub issue yet. That's just something I'll do later. For now, just give me one GitHub issue draft that comprehensively captures where we've landed and all of the nuance from our conversation. The GitHub issue doesn't need to give a history of everything that was considered. It just needs to give our final agreed understanding, not a history of the conversation.
Awesome, thanks for doing that. I haven't read that GitHub issue comprehensively, and I don't think I will, because I've got limited cognitive energy to expend as a human, and you as an AI agent can create a virtually limitless supply of documents for me to review. So I'll take it on faith that that GitHub issue's draft by and large captures our conversation. For auditing purposes, can you create that GitHub issue in GitHub on the repo, but can you also take the full transcripts of this conversation and attach it as a link to that GitHub issue as well, so that there's an audit trail between this conversation and the GitHub issue? I know the transcript for this conversation should be saved in its own branch already, given the hook that was set up previously. So ideally you should be able to just link that conversation to the GitHub issue.

content.text:
I've read issues 2 and 3, issue 3's two comments, the repo, and the transcripts of the last two sessions. Two things from those carry into this session:

- Last session offered to merge the file list with the ownership table, but you never decided. That's Q4.
- You have a rule that issues don't record how you work with agents. So the issue 3 comment at the end will only say the scaffold is committed.

I'll ask about the branch, commit and issue comment once the scaffold is agreed. Round 1:

❓ **Q1** - **Scope**: Should the file cover anything beyond issue 3 and its comments (purpose, file list, philosophy, ownership, diagram)? For example, conventions for agents working here: branches, commit messages, how issues are written, audit-trail links.

➡️ No. Issue 3 says the file sets out the philosophy. Conventions can be a later issue.

---

❓ **Q2** - **Overall shape**:
- **A. Flat:** one section per idea, in #2's order: the two spaces, requirements, contract, steering, implementation, ownership.
- **B. Nested by space, like the diagram:** Problem space > Requirements; Contract alone as the boundary; Solution space > Steering, Implementation.
- **C. By task:** "Working on requirements", "Working on the implementation", "When to stop and ask".

➡️ A. It's closest to "the philosophy as #2 states it" and stays shallow. B adds a heading level for little gain. C means writing procedures #2 never states.

---

❓ **Q3** - **Opening**: After `# Contributing`, is the purpose an unheaded opening paragraph or a `## Purpose` section?

➡️ An unheaded paragraph. Comment 2 says the file *opens* with its purpose, and a sentence or two doesn't need a heading.

---

❓ **Q4** - **File list**: Which files does it name, and does it double as the ownership table?

➡️ It names `README.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `REQUIREMENTS.md`, `CONTRACT.md`, `STEERING.md` and "the implementation". The implementation gets no file names or technology. It also isn't described as "every other file", because that would quietly make `.claude/` agent-owned.

It leaves out four things:
- `.claude/`, since its ownership is undecided
- `PRD.md` and `.config/configuration.winget`, since naming them amounts to a note about the move
- the `agent-transcripts` branch

Merge it with ownership: one table (file, what it's for, owner) with the three kinds of ownership under it. That way an agent learns in one place what each file is and whether it may touch it.

This needs one new decision: #2 gives `CLAUDE.md` no owner. I'd make it Shared, like `README.md`.

---

❓ **Q5** - **Diagram placement**:
- **A:** near the top, right after the file table, as an overview
- **B:** at the end, as a summary

➡️ A. The reader sees the whole shape first, and each later section zooms into one box.

---

❓ **Q6** - **Examples**: Every example must be an analogy clearly unrelated to this repo, like `CONTRACT.md` ↔ a `.pyi` stub.
- **A:** one running analogy, that Python library, used inline wherever a section needs an example
- **B:** a different analogy for each section
- **C:** one "Analogy" section that maps every file to the library, with no examples anywhere else

➡️ A. One world keeps the pieces lined up: requirements are what the library's users need, the contract is the stub, steering is something like `NEVER add a runtime dependency`, and the implementation is the `.py` source. The scaffold only marks which sections carry an example.

---

❓ **Q7** - **Comment format and lifetime**:
- **A:** an HTML comment `<!-- … -->` under each heading, deleted once that section is written
- **B:** HTML comments kept permanently, as each section's remit
- **C:** visible italic placeholders, which also show on GitHub's rendered page

➡️ A. Agents read the raw file, so "hidden" comments aren't hidden from them, and permanent ones would repeat the content. The trade-off: GitHub's rendered view shows only the headings until the content is written.

---

❓ **Q8** - **What the comments say**:
- **A:** a one-line remit for each heading
- **B:** a short list of every point each heading must cover, plus one short block at the top for issue 3's rules for the whole file: no "you", unrelated analogies only, no links to the three new files, no note about the move, none of #2's open questions answered, nothing on how humans work with agents

➡️ B, with each comment a line or two. Every point in issue 3 then has a home you can check at a glance.

---

With every recommendation taken, the top level looks like this (wording is a placeholder):

```
# Contributing
  (purpose paragraph)
## Files and ownership
## Diagram
## Problem space and solution space
## Requirements (`REQUIREMENTS.md`)
## Contract (`CONTRACT.md`)
## Steering (`STEERING.md`)
## Implementation
```

Subheadings and heading wording come in round 2. You can answer by number, and "rest as recommended" is fine.

# Contributing

## Purpose of this file

_States that this file tells agents how to interact with this
repository when they contribute to it, and that it doesn't
cover how humans work with agents._

## Files and ownership

_One table of the major files and the implementation: what
each is for, and its ownership. `README.md`,
`CONTRIBUTING.md`, `CLAUDE.md` and `CONTRACT.md` have shared
ownership. `REQUIREMENTS.md` is human-owned at its top level,
with shared ownership below. `STEERING.md` is human-owned.
The implementation is agent-owned; its row names no files or
technology, and doesn't call it "every other file"._

### Human-owned

_What human-owned means: content that comes entirely from the
human._

### Shared ownership

_What shared ownership means: content created collaboratively
by the human and agents. The human decides what goes in and
understands all of it, so agents never build up content the
human hasn't had the time or space to understand: no
understanding debt._

### Agent-owned

_What agent-owned means: content created entirely by the
agent. The human isn't expected to understand all of it, or
any of it, and never edits it._

## Diagram

_A Mermaid diagram of the files and how they relate. It shows
`README.md` and `CLAUDE.md` leading here, this file setting
the rules, the requirements tree, the contract on the
boundary, the steering keywords and how binding each is, and
the implementation, each in its space. Each arrow is labeled
with its relationship, and colors show the three kinds of
ownership, with a legend. Renders on GitHub._

## The two spaces

_The problem space is what's needed, in `REQUIREMENTS.md`.
The solution space is how it's built: the implementation,
guided by `STEERING.md`. `CONTRACT.md` sits on the boundary.
The split is strict: requirements never specify or prescribe
the solution's tech stack, and steering never states a
need._

## Problem space

### Requirements (`REQUIREMENTS.md`)

_A tree of requirements. The top level comes entirely from
the human. Every other requirement is derived from the one
above it and cites that parent's ID, so every line traces
back to the top. The human derives the lower levels, with an
agent's help if wanted, and decides what goes in and
understands every line. A requirement is broken down only
when it needs more detail: the levels aren't the same
content restated, and no bottom level captures everything._

## Boundary

### Contract (`CONTRACT.md`)

_The interface through which the human uses the result.
Narrow, following the deep modules principle. Derived from
the requirements as a whole, at every level. Cites no
requirement IDs, with the reason. Agreed like a
requirement._

## Solution space

### Steering (`STEERING.md`)

_The human's guidance on how the implementation is built:
solution space only, written by the human. A bullet list in
which every bullet starts with one of five all-caps
keywords. Covers only what sits behind the contract, so it
can't contradict the contract._

#### Keywords

_A table of `ALWAYS` / `NEVER`, `FAVOR` / `DISFAVOR` and
`CONSIDER`: what each is, and whether and how the
implementation can depart from it._

#### Conflicts

_Why steering can't directly contradict a requirement, and
what a seeming contradiction means: something is in the
wrong file. `ALWAYS` and `NEVER` rules can still rule out
every implementation that meets the requirements. Either
way, the agent stops and asks the human instead of breaking
a rule or missing a requirement._

### Implementation

_Agent-owned. It implements the contract and meets every
requirement, at every level. The agent chooses the approach
and technology from the requirements, the contract and the
steering; the human shapes it only through those three
files._

## Analogies

_Three analogies, each explicitly unrelated to this
repository and giving no direction for it. They're the
file's only examples. Each walks through every part above,
in order: files and ownership, the two spaces, requirements,
contract, steering and implementation._

### A Python library

_The contract is its `.pyi` stub files: the public
signatures, and nothing about how they're implemented._

### A web service with an HTTP API

_The contract is its OpenAPI spec._

### A mobile app

_The contract is the screens and actions its users see._

## Traceability

_The overarching rule that every change to this repository
is traceable, through the audit trails below._

### Commits, issues and agent transcripts

_All work starts from an issue. Every commit message links
that issue and the transcript of the agent session that
made the commit. Every issue links the transcripts of the
sessions that drafted or changed it. Transcripts live on the
`agent-transcripts` branch, one file per session, which
`.claude/hooks/save-transcript.sh` updates after every
turn._

# Contributing

## Purpose of this file

_States that this file tells agents how to interact with this
repository when they contribute to it, and that it doesn't
cover how humans work with agents._

## Files and ownership

_One table of the major files and the implementation: what
each is for, and its ownership. `README.md`,
`CONTRIBUTING.md`, `CLAUDE.md` and `CONTRACT.md` have shared
ownership. `REQUIREMENTS.md` is human-owned at its top level,
with shared ownership below. `STEERING.md` is human-owned.
The implementation is agent-owned; its row names no files or
technology, and doesn't call it "every other file"._

### Human-owned

_What human-owned means: content that comes entirely from the
human._

### Shared ownership

_What shared ownership means: content created collaboratively
by the human and agents. The human decides what goes in and
understands all of it, so agents never build up content the
human hasn't had the time or space to understand: no
understanding debt._

### Agent-owned

_What agent-owned means: content created entirely by the
agent. The human isn't expected to understand all of it, or
any of it, and never edits it._

## Diagram

_A Mermaid diagram of the files and how they relate. It shows
`README.md` and `CLAUDE.md` leading here, this file setting
the rules, the requirements tree, the contract on the
boundary, the steering keywords and how binding each is, and
the implementation, each in its space. Each arrow is labeled
with its relationship, and colors show the three kinds of
ownership, with a legend. Renders on GitHub._

## The two spaces

_The problem space is what's needed, in `REQUIREMENTS.md`.
The solution space is how it's built: the implementation,
guided by `STEERING.md`. `CONTRACT.md` sits on the boundary.
The split is strict: requirements never specify or prescribe
the solution's tech stack, and steering never states a
need._

## Problem space

### Requirements (`REQUIREMENTS.md`)

_A tree of requirements. The top level comes entirely from
the human. Every other requirement is derived from the one
above it and cites that parent's ID, so every line traces
back to the top. The human derives the lower levels, with an
agent's help if wanted, and decides what goes in and
understands every line. A requirement is broken down only
when it needs more detail: the levels aren't the same
content restated, and no bottom level captures everything._

## Boundary

### Contract (`CONTRACT.md`)

_The interface through which the human uses the result.
Narrow, following the deep modules principle. Derived from
the requirements as a whole, at every level. Cites no
requirement IDs, with the reason. Agreed like a
requirement._

## Solution space

### Steering (`STEERING.md`)

_The human's guidance on how the implementation is built:
solution space only, written by the human. A bullet list in
which every bullet starts with one of five all-caps
keywords. Covers only what sits behind the contract, so it
can't contradict the contract._

#### Keywords

_A table of `ALWAYS` / `NEVER`, `FAVOR` / `DISFAVOR` and
`CONSIDER`: what each is, and whether and how the
implementation can depart from it._

#### Conflicts

_Why steering can't directly contradict a requirement, and
what a seeming contradiction means: something is in the
wrong file. `ALWAYS` and `NEVER` rules can still rule out
every implementation that meets the requirements. Either
way, the agent stops and asks the human instead of breaking
a rule or missing a requirement._

### Implementation

_Agent-owned. It implements the contract and meets every
requirement, at every level. The agent chooses the approach
and technology from the requirements, the contract and the
steering; the human shapes it only through those three
files._

## Analogies

_Three analogies, each explicitly unrelated to this
repository and giving no direction for it. They're the
file's only examples. Each walks through every part above,
in order: files and ownership, the two spaces, requirements,
contract, steering and implementation._

### A Python library

_The contract is its `.pyi` stub files: the public
signatures, and nothing about how they're implemented._

### A web service with an HTTP API

_The contract is its OpenAPI spec._

### A mobile app

_The contract is the screens and actions its users see._

## Traceability

_The overarching rule that every change to this repository
is traceable, through the audit trails below._

### Commits, issues and agent transcripts

_All work starts from an issue. Every commit message links
that issue and the transcript of the agent session that
made the commit. Every issue links the transcripts of the
sessions that drafted or changed it. Transcripts live on the
`agent-transcripts` branch, one file per session, which
`.claude/hooks/save-transcript.sh` updates after every
turn._
```

# Contributing

## Purpose of this file

_States that this file tells agents how to interact with this
repository when they contribute to it, and that it doesn't
cover how humans work with agents._

## Glossary

- **Problem space**: _What's needed, independent of how it's
  met._
- **Solution space**: _How what's needed is met._
- **Contract**: _The interface through which the solution is
  used, saying nothing about how it's built._
- **Human-owned**: _Comes entirely from the human._
- **Shared ownership**: _Created collaboratively by the human
  and agents. The human decides what goes in and understands
  all of it, so that XXXX debt is avoided._
- **Agent-owned**: _Created entirely by the agent. The human
  isn't expected to understand all of it, or any of it, and
  never edits it._
- **Steering keyword**: _The all-caps word that starts each
  steering bullet and says whether the implementation can
  depart from it. There are five:_
  - **`ALWAYS`**: _A rule about what the implementation always
    does. No departure._
  - **`NEVER`**: _A rule about what the implementation never
    does. No departure._
  - **`FAVOR`**: _A preference for something. The
    implementation can depart from it, with a stated reason._
  - **`DISFAVOR`**: _A preference against something. The
    implementation can depart from it, with a stated reason._
  - **`CONSIDER`**: _Inspiration, not a preference. The
    implementation can ignore it without giving a reason._

## File layout and ownership

_A folder tree of the fixed files this file names:
`README.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, `CLAUDE.md`,
`REQUIREMENTS.md`, `CONTRACT.md` and `STEERING.md` at the
root, and `.claude/hooks/save-transcript.sh`. Nothing the
implementation adds appears in it, so it never needs
updating as the implementation grows._

_A table of the major files and the implementation: what
each is for, and its ownership. `README.md`,
`CONTRIBUTING.md`, `CLAUDE.md` and `CONTRACT.md` have shared
ownership. `REQUIREMENTS.md` is human-owned at its top
level, with shared ownership below. `STEERING.md` is
human-owned. The implementation is agent-owned; its row
names no files or technology, and doesn't call it "every
other file"._

## Diagram

_A Mermaid diagram of the files and how they relate, laid
out with ELK. It shows `README.md` and `CLAUDE.md` leading
here, this file setting the rules, the requirements tree,
the contract on the boundary, the steering keywords and how
binding each is, and the implementation, each in its space.
Each arrow is labeled with its relationship, and colors show
the three kinds of ownership, with a legend. Renders on
GitHub._

## The two spaces

_The split between the problem space and the solution space
is strict: requirements never specify or prescribe the
solution's tech stack, and steering never states a need. The
contract sits on the boundary between them._

## Problem space files

### Requirements (`REQUIREMENTS.md`)

_A tree of requirements. The top level comes entirely from
the human. Every other requirement is derived from the one
above it and cites that parent's ID, so every line traces
back to the top. The human derives the lower levels, with an
agent's help if wanted, and decides what goes in and
understands every line. A requirement is broken down only
when it needs more detail: the levels aren't the same
content restated, and no bottom level captures everything._

## Boundary

### Contract (`CONTRACT.md`)

_Holds the contract: narrow, following the deep modules
principle, and derived from the requirements as a whole, at
every level. Agreed like a requirement._

## Solution space files

### Steering (`STEERING.md`)

_The human's guidance on how the implementation is built:
solution space only, written by the human. A bullet list in
which every bullet starts with a steering keyword: `ALWAYS`,
`NEVER`, `FAVOR`, `DISFAVOR` or `CONSIDER`. Covers only what
sits behind the contract, so it can't contradict the
contract._

#### Conflicts

_Why steering can't directly contradict a requirement, and
what a seeming contradiction means: something is in the
wrong file. `ALWAYS` and `NEVER` rules can still rule out
every implementation that meets the requirements._

### Implementation

_Agent-owned. It implements the contract and meets every
requirement, at every level. The agent chooses the approach
and technology from the requirements, the contract and the
steering; the human shapes it only through those three
files._

## Analogies

_One line: the analogies below are explicitly unrelated to
this repository and give no direction for it._

### A Python library

_The analogy applied to the whole structure, part by part.
The contract is the library's `.pyi` stub files: the public
signatures, and nothing about how they're implemented._

### A web service with an HTTP API

_The analogy applied to the whole structure, part by part.
The contract is the service's OpenAPI spec._

### A mobile app

_The analogy applied to the whole structure, part by part.
The contract is the screens and actions its users see._

## Traceability

_The overarching rule that every change to this repository
is traceable, through the audit trails below._

### Commits, issues and agent transcripts

_All work starts from an issue. Every commit message links
that issue and the transcript of the agent session that
made the commit. Every issue links the transcripts of the
sessions that drafted or changed it. Transcripts live on the
`agent-transcripts` branch, one file per session, which
`.claude/hooks/save-transcript.sh` updates after every
turn._

# Contributing

## Purpose of this file

_States that this file tells agents how to interact with this
repository when they contribute to it, and that it doesn't
cover how humans work with agents._

## Files and ownership

_One table of the major files and the implementation: what
each is for, and its ownership. `README.md`,
`CONTRIBUTING.md`, `CLAUDE.md` and `CONTRACT.md` have shared
ownership. `REQUIREMENTS.md` is human-owned at its top level,
with shared ownership below. `STEERING.md` is human-owned.
The implementation is agent-owned; its row names no files or
technology, and doesn't call it "every other file"._

### Human-owned

_What human-owned means: content that comes entirely from the
human._

### Shared ownership

_What shared ownership means: content created collaboratively
by the human and agents. The human decides what goes in and
understands all of it, so agents never build up content the
human hasn't had the time or space to understand: no
understanding debt._

### Agent-owned

_What agent-owned means: content created entirely by the
agent. The human isn't expected to understand all of it, or
any of it, and never edits it._

## Diagram

_A Mermaid diagram of the files and how they relate. It shows
`README.md` and `CLAUDE.md` leading here, this file setting
the rules, the requirements tree, the contract on the
boundary, the steering keywords and how binding each is, and
the implementation, each in its space. Each arrow is labeled
with its relationship, and colors show the three kinds of
ownership, with a legend. Renders on GitHub._

## The two spaces

_The problem space is what's needed, in `REQUIREMENTS.md`.
The solution space is how it's built: the implementation,
guided by `STEERING.md`. `CONTRACT.md` sits on the boundary.
The split is strict: requirements never specify or prescribe
the solution's tech stack, and steering never states a
need._

## Problem space

### Requirements (`REQUIREMENTS.md`)

_A tree of requirements. The top level comes entirely from
the human. Every other requirement is derived from the one
above it and cites that parent's ID, so every line traces
back to the top. The human derives the lower levels, with an
agent's help if wanted, and decides what goes in and
understands every line. A requirement is broken down only
when it needs more detail: the levels aren't the same
content restated, and no bottom level captures everything._

## Boundary

### Contract (`CONTRACT.md`)

_The interface through which the human uses the result.
Narrow, following the deep modules principle. Derived from
the requirements as a whole, at every level. Cites no
requirement IDs, with the reason. Agreed like a
requirement._

## Solution space

### Steering (`STEERING.md`)

_The human's guidance on how the implementation is built:
solution space only, written by the human. A bullet list in
which every bullet starts with one of five all-caps
keywords. Covers only what sits behind the contract, so it
can't contradict the contract._

#### Keywords

_A table of `ALWAYS` / `NEVER`, `FAVOR` / `DISFAVOR` and
`CONSIDER`: what each is, and whether and how the
implementation can depart from it._

#### Conflicts

_Why steering can't directly contradict a requirement, and
what a seeming contradiction means: something is in the
wrong file. `ALWAYS` and `NEVER` rules can still rule out
every implementation that meets the requirements. Either
way, the agent stops and asks the human instead of breaking
a rule or missing a requirement._

### Implementation

_Agent-owned. It implements the contract and meets every
requirement, at every level. The agent chooses the approach
and technology from the requirements, the contract and the
steering; the human shapes it only through those three
files._

## Analogies

_Three analogies, each explicitly unrelated to this
repository and giving no direction for it. They're the
file's only examples. Each walks through every part above,
in order: files and ownership, the two spaces, requirements,
contract, steering and implementation._

### A Python library

_The contract is its `.pyi` stub files: the public
signatures, and nothing about how they're implemented._

### A web service with an HTTP API

_The contract is its OpenAPI spec._

### A mobile app

_The contract is the screens and actions its users see._

## Traceability

_The overarching rule that every change to this repository
is traceable, through the audit trails below._

### Commits, issues and agent transcripts

_All work starts from an issue. Every commit message links
that issue and the transcript of the agent session that
made the commit. Every issue links the transcripts of the
sessions that drafted or changed it. Transcripts live on the
`agent-transcripts` branch, one file per session, which
`.claude/hooks/save-transcript.sh` updates after every
turn._

This also fits the owner's memory: "comprehension" is a synonym for "understanding", which is probably why they remember it as not being "understanding debt".
  
  **1. Term:** comprehension debt. It's written lowercase in running text, like "technical debt", and is sometimes capitalized in headlines.
  
  **2. Definition:** Comprehension debt is the growing gap between how much code (or other content) exists in a system and how much of it any person actually understands. It builds up when AI produces code faster than people can read and understand it.
  - Jason Gorman's original wording: "When teams produce code faster than they can understand it, it creates what I've been calling 'comprehension debt'."
  - Addy Osmani's wording: "the growing gap between how much code exists in your system and how much of it any human being genuinely understands."
  
  **3. Origin:** Jason Gorman (Codemanship) coined it on 30 Sep 2025. He doesn't explicitly claim to have invented it ("what I've been calling…"), but later sources credit him. Addy Osmani popularized it in March 2026, and O'Reilly Radar reposted his piece. One caveat: Osmani's opening line describes it as a "hidden cost to human intelligence and memory", which blurs it with the near-miss sense in item 5. If you quote a definition, use the "gap" wording above.
  
  **4. Sources** (all opened directly except where noted):
  - Gorman, "Comprehension Debt: The Ticking Time Bomb of LLM-Generated Code", 30 Sep 2025: https://codemanship.wordpress.com/2025/09/30/comprehension-debt-the-ticking-time-bomb-of-llm-generated-code/
  - Osmani, "Comprehension Debt", 14 Mar 2026: https://addyosmani.com/blog/comprehension-debt/
    - O'Reilly Radar repost, 13 Apr 2026: https://www.oreilly.com/radar/comprehension-debt-the-hidden-cost-of-ai-generated-code/
  - Muhammad Ovais Ahmad, "Comprehension Debt in GenAI-Assisted Software Engineering Projects", arXiv:2604.13277, 14 Apr 2026: https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.13277
  - Faros AI (a vendor), 29 Sep 2026: https://www.faros.ai/blog/comprehension-debt-in-software-engineering. It says "Comprehension debt, also referred to as cognitive debt."
  
  **5. Confidence and competitors:** I'm fairly confident (about 85%) that comprehension debt is the term that names exactly this concept.
  
  The closest competitor is **"cognitive debt"**. It's just as prominent in well-known venues, and some writers (Osmani, Faros) treat it as a synonym:
  - Margaret-Anne Storey defines it as "the accumulated gap between a system's evolving structure and a team's shared understanding…" (blog posts of 9 and 18 Feb 2026: https://margaretstorey.com/blog/2026/02/18/cognitive-debt-revisited/).
  - Simon Willison picked it up (15 Feb 2026), as did Martin Fowler (2 Apr 2026: https://martinfowler.com/fragments/2026-04-02.html).
  - The Thoughtworks Technology Radar Vol. 34 made it a theme (press release, 15 Apr 2026: https://www.thoughtworks.com/about-us/news/2026/combat-ai-cognitive-debt-radar-v34).
  
  It fits less well for two reasons:
  - **It's ambiguous.** Its best-known AI-era origin is the MIT Media Lab paper "Your Brain on ChatGPT: Accumulation of Cognitive Debt…" (Kosmyna et al., 10 Jun 2025: https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08872). That paper is about people's own thinking, memory and learning weakening when they rely on AI, which is exactly the near-miss you described. Storey's first post on it links to that study.
  - **It's broader.** Even in the software sense, it means a team's eroding shared understanding of a system ("lives in people"). It doesn't specifically mean content the responsible person hasn't read and understood.

  - **"verification debt"**: Werner Vogels, AWS re:Invent keynote, Dec 2025. It's about code reaching production before anyone validates it, so it's about checking rather than understanding. I confirmed this only through secondhand reports.

  - **"knowledge debt"**, **"epistemic debt"** and **"copilot debt"**: only niche usage turned up.

# Contributing

## Purpose of this file

_States that this file tells agents how to interact with this
repository when they contribute to it, and that it doesn't
cover how humans work with agents._

## Glossary

- **Problem space**: _What's needed, independent of how it's
  met._
- **Solution space**: _How what's needed is met._
- **Contract**: _The interface through which the solution is
  used, saying nothing about how it's built._
- **Human-owned**: _Comes entirely from the human._
- **Shared ownership**: _Created collaboratively by the human
  and agents. The human decides what goes in and understands
  all of it, so that XXXX debt is avoided._
- **Agent-owned**: _Created entirely by the agent. The human
  isn't expected to understand all of it, or any of it, and
  never edits it._
- **Steering keyword**: _The all-caps word that starts each
  steering bullet and says whether the implementation can
  depart from it. There are five:_
  - **`ALWAYS`**: _A rule about what the implementation always
    does. No departure._
  - **`NEVER`**: _A rule about what the implementation never
    does. No departure._
  - **`FAVOR`**: _A preference for something. The
    implementation can depart from it, with a stated reason._
  - **`DISFAVOR`**: _A preference against something. The
    implementation can depart from it, with a stated reason._
  - **`CONSIDER`**: _Inspiration, not a preference. The
    implementation can ignore it without giving a reason._

## File layout and ownership

_A folder tree of the fixed files this file names:
`README.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, `CLAUDE.md`,
`REQUIREMENTS.md`, `CONTRACT.md` and `STEERING.md` at the
root, and `.claude/hooks/save-transcript.sh`. Nothing the
implementation adds appears in it, so it never needs
updating as the implementation grows._

_A table of the major files and the implementation: what
each is for, and its ownership. `README.md`,
`CONTRIBUTING.md`, `CLAUDE.md` and `CONTRACT.md` have shared
ownership. `REQUIREMENTS.md` is human-owned at its top
level, with shared ownership below. `STEERING.md` is
human-owned. The implementation is agent-owned; its row
names no files or technology, and doesn't call it "every
other file"._

## Diagram

_A Mermaid diagram of the files and how they relate, laid
out with ELK. It shows `README.md` and `CLAUDE.md` leading
here, this file setting the rules, the requirements tree,
the contract on the boundary, the steering keywords and how
binding each is, and the implementation, each in its space.
Each arrow is labeled with its relationship, and colors show
the three kinds of ownership, with a legend. Renders on
GitHub._

## The two spaces

_The split between the problem space and the solution space
is strict: requirements never specify or prescribe the
solution's tech stack, and steering never states a need. The
contract sits on the boundary between them._

## Problem space files

### Requirements (`REQUIREMENTS.md`)

_A tree of requirements. The top level comes entirely from
the human. Every other requirement is derived from the one
above it and cites that parent's ID, so every line traces
back to the top. The human derives the lower levels, with an
agent's help if wanted, and decides what goes in and
understands every line. A requirement is broken down only
when it needs more detail: the levels aren't the same
content restated, and no bottom level captures everything._

## Boundary

### Contract (`CONTRACT.md`)

_Holds the contract: narrow, following the deep modules
principle, and derived from the requirements as a whole, at
every level. Agreed like a requirement._

## Solution space files

### Steering (`STEERING.md`)

_The human's guidance on how the implementation is built:
solution space only, written by the human. A bullet list in
which every bullet starts with a steering keyword: `ALWAYS`,
`NEVER`, `FAVOR`, `DISFAVOR` or `CONSIDER`. Covers only what
sits behind the contract, so it can't contradict the
contract._

#### Conflicts

_Why steering can't directly contradict a requirement, and
what a seeming contradiction means: something is in the
wrong file. `ALWAYS` and `NEVER` rules can still rule out
every implementation that meets the requirements._

### Implementation

_Agent-owned. It implements the contract and meets every
requirement, at every level. The agent chooses the approach
and technology from the requirements, the contract and the
steering; the human shapes it only through those three
files._

## Analogies

_One line: the analogies below are explicitly unrelated to
this repository and give no direction for it._

### A Python library

_The analogy applied to the whole structure, part by part.
The contract is the library's `.pyi` stub files: the public
signatures, and nothing about how they're implemented._

### A web service with an HTTP API

_The analogy applied to the whole structure, part by part.
The contract is the service's OpenAPI spec._

### A mobile app

_The analogy applied to the whole structure, part by part.
The contract is the screens and actions its users see._

## Traceability

_The overarching rule that every change to this repository
is traceable, through the audit trails below._

### Commits, issues and agent transcripts

_All work starts from an issue. Every commit message links
that issue and the transcript of the agent session that
made the commit. Every issue links the transcripts of the
sessions that drafted or changed it. Transcripts live on the
`agent-transcripts` branch, one file per session, which
`.claude/hooks/save-transcript.sh` updates after every
turn._

  ## GitHub Mermaid + ELK: findings as of 2026-10-23
  
  **Short answer:** github.com now renders Mermaid diagrams with Mermaid 12.2.0, which has ELK built in. The frontmatter `config: layout: elk` works. No GitHub announcement or changelog entry covers this. The evidence is GitHub's own live renderer code, read with plain HTTP fetches; nothing was rendered in a browser. No files were created and no repos were touched.
  
  ### 1. Does GitHub support ELK, and with what syntax?
  Yes. Mermaid blocks on github.com render in an iframe from `https://viewscreen.githubusercontent.com/markdown/mermaid` (marked `data-deploy-env="production"`). That page loads `/static/assets/mermaidMarkdown-5b99bd9a2037271fa4cf.js`, which shows:
  - **Version:** Mermaid's render call includes its own version string: `renderer.draw(e,t,"12.2.0",C)`.
  - **ELK is registered by default:** the default layout list holds dagre, swimlane and cose-bilkent, then adds `elk` (`elk.layered`) and `elk.stress`/`force`/`mrtree`/`sporeOverlap`/`box`/`rectpacking`.
  - **The ELK code is served:** the lazily loaded ELK file `1620-5b99bd9a2037271fa4cf.js` returns HTTP 200 (about 1.5 MB) and contains the ELK engine (`org.eclipse.elk` appears 342 times).
  - **GitHub doesn't block or override the setting.** GitHub's settings call is `initialize({secure:["secure","securityLevel","startOnLoad","maxTextSize"], securityLevel:"antiscript", flowchart:{diagramPadding:48}, …, theme})`. It doesn't set `layout`, and `layout` isn't on the locked list, so a diagram's frontmatter can set it. GitHub's wrapper only HTML-decodes the diagram text before passing it to Mermaid, so frontmatter survives.
  - **ELK is already the default:** the build's default settings say `layout:"elk"`. Flowcharts on GitHub now get ELK even without any config.
  
  Syntax that works (recommended):
  ````
  ```mermaid
  ---
  config:
    layout: elk
  ---
  flowchart TD
    A --> B
  ```
  ````
  Two other forms also work in this build. The `flowchart-elk` header is still detected and switches to ELK. `%%{init: {"layout": "elk"}}%%` is still parsed, though Mermaid prefers frontmatter. The old `flowchart: {defaultRenderer: "elk"}` setting was removed in 12.0 and is now ignored.
  
  ### 2. What happens when ELK isn't available?
  The diagram silently falls back to dagre and no error is shown.
  - In Mermaid 11.16.1, ELK isn't in the default layout list. Asking for `elk` (via frontmatter, `flowchart-elk` or `defaultRenderer`) only triggers `log.warn("Layout algorithm elk is not registered. Using dagre as fallback.")`.
  - Mermaid's default log level is 5 (fatal only), and GitHub doesn't change it, so even that warning never appears in the console.
  - GitHub shows an error ("Unable to render rich display", the error message, and a link to the docs) only when Mermaid actually fails, such as on a syntax error. A missing layout never gets that far.
  - The same silent fallback still applies on github.com today for a misspelled layout name. It also applies in any viewer still on Mermaid 11 without the separate ELK package, such as GitHub Enterprise Server or IDE previews (I didn't check those). Mermaid 12's "tiny" build also falls back to dagre.
  
  ### 3. Which Mermaid version does GitHub use?
  **Now:** 12.2.0, the full build (not "tiny"), published to npm 2026-10-13. It was therefore deployed within the last ten days. Since 12.0.0, ELK is bundled and `@mermaid-js/layout-elk` is no longer needed.
  
  **Before:** users reading GitHub's `info` diagram reported 10.0.2 (2023 to Jan 2024), 10.8.0 (Feb 2024), 11.4.1 (2025-04-08) and 11.16.1 (2026-08-20). In 11.x, ELK required the separate `@mermaid-js/layout-elk` package to be registered, and GitHub never did that. ELK requests on GitHub before this upgrade therefore silently rendered with dagre.

  - Community discussion #70672, user-reported versions (2023 to 2026-08-20; no staff): https://github.com/orgs/community/discussions/70672
  - Community discussion #203196, the "Unable to render rich display" error and the viewscreen host (Jul–Sep 2026): https://github.com/orgs/community/discussions/203196
  - Mermaid 12.0.0 release notes (ELK bundled and default; tiny build falls back to dagre; `defaultRenderer` removed): https://github.com/mermaid-js/mermaid/releases/tag/mermaid%4012.0.0

**The term is "comprehension debt":** the gap between how much content exists and how much of it a person actually understands. Jason Gorman coined it in September 2025, and Addy Osmani made it popular in March 2026. The closest rival, "cognitive debt", also means people's own thinking getting weaker when they lean on AI, so it's ambiguous here.

**ELK works on GitHub.** About ten days ago GitHub moved to Mermaid 12.2.0, which has ELK built in, so setting `layout: elk` in the diagram's settings block takes effect. If ELK ever stops being available, the diagram quietly falls back to the default layout rather than breaking. This comes from reading GitHub's renderer code; nobody has rendered a test diagram yet.

# Contributing

## Purpose of this file

_States that this file tells agents how to interact with this
repository when they contribute to it, and that it doesn't
cover how humans work with agents._

## Glossary

- **Problem space**: _What's needed, independent of how it's
  met._
- **Solution space**: _How what's needed is met._
- **Contract**: _The interface through which the solution is
  used, saying nothing about how it's built._
- **Human-owned**: _Comes entirely from the human._
- **Shared ownership**: _Created collaboratively by the human
  and agents. The human decides what goes in and understands
  all of it, so that comprehension debt is avoided._
- **Agent-owned**: _Created entirely by the agent. The human
  isn't expected to understand all of it, or any of it, and
  never edits it._
- **Steering keyword**: _The all-caps word that starts each
  steering bullet and says whether the implementation can
  depart from it. There are five:_
  - **`ALWAYS`**: _A rule about what the implementation always
    does. No departure._
  - **`NEVER`**: _A rule about what the implementation never
    does. No departure._
  - **`FAVOR`**: _A preference for something. The
    implementation can depart from it, with a stated reason._
  - **`DISFAVOR`**: _A preference against something. The
    implementation can depart from it, with a stated reason._
  - **`CONSIDER`**: _Inspiration, not a preference. The
    implementation can ignore it without giving a reason._

## File layout and ownership

_A folder tree of the fixed files this file names:
`README.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, `CLAUDE.md`,
`REQUIREMENTS.md`, `CONTRACT.md` and `STEERING.md` at the
root, and `.claude/hooks/save-transcript.sh`. Nothing the
implementation adds appears in it, so it never needs
updating as the implementation grows._

_A table of the major files and the implementation: what
each is for, and its ownership. `README.md`,
`CONTRIBUTING.md`, `CLAUDE.md` and `CONTRACT.md` have shared
ownership. `REQUIREMENTS.md` is human-owned at its top
level, with shared ownership below. `STEERING.md` is
human-owned. The implementation is agent-owned; its row
names no files or technology, and doesn't call it "every
other file"._

## Diagram

_A Mermaid diagram of the files and how they relate, laid
out with ELK. It shows `README.md` and `CLAUDE.md` leading
here, this file setting the rules, the requirements tree,
the contract on the boundary, the steering keywords and how
binding each is, and the implementation, each in its space.
Each arrow is labeled with its relationship, and colors show
the three kinds of ownership, with a legend. Renders on
GitHub._

## The two spaces

_The split between the problem space and the solution space
is strict: requirements never specify or prescribe the
solution's tech stack, and steering never states a need. The
contract sits on the boundary between them._

## Problem space files

### Requirements (`REQUIREMENTS.md`)

_A tree of requirements. The top level comes entirely from
the human. Every other requirement is derived from the one
above it and cites that parent's ID, so every line traces
back to the top. The human derives the lower levels, with an
agent's help if wanted, and decides what goes in and
understands every line. A requirement is broken down only
when it needs more detail: the levels aren't the same
content restated, and no bottom level captures everything._

## Boundary

### Contract (`CONTRACT.md`)

_Holds the contract: narrow, following the deep modules
principle, and derived from the requirements as a whole, at
every level. Agreed like a requirement._

## Solution space files

### Steering (`STEERING.md`)

_The human's guidance on how the implementation is built:
solution space only, written by the human. A bullet list in
which every bullet starts with a steering keyword: `ALWAYS`,
`NEVER`, `FAVOR`, `DISFAVOR` or `CONSIDER`. Covers only what
sits behind the contract, so it can't contradict the
contract._

#### Conflicts

_Why steering can't directly contradict a requirement, and
what a seeming contradiction means: something is in the
wrong file. `ALWAYS` and `NEVER` rules can still rule out
every implementation that meets the requirements._

### Implementation

_Agent-owned. It implements the contract and meets every
requirement, at every level. The agent chooses the approach
and technology from the requirements, the contract and the
steering; the human shapes it only through those three
files._

## Analogies

_One line: the analogies below are explicitly unrelated to
this repository and give no direction for it._

### A Python library

_The analogy applied to the whole structure, part by part.
The contract is the library's `.pyi` stub files: the public
signatures, and nothing about how they're implemented._

### A web service with an HTTP API

_The analogy applied to the whole structure, part by part.
The contract is the service's OpenAPI spec._

### A mobile app

_The analogy applied to the whole structure, part by part.
The contract is the screens and actions its users see._

## Traceability

_The overarching rule that every change to this repository
is traceable, through the audit trails below._

### Commits, issues and agent transcripts

_All work starts from an issue. Every commit message links
that issue and the transcript of the agent session that
made the commit. Every issue links the transcripts of the
sessions that drafted or changed it. Transcripts live on the
`agent-transcripts` branch, one file per session, which
`.claude/hooks/save-transcript.sh` updates after every
turn._
```

- **The two spaces:** it now holds only the strict split and the boundary. The glossary defines the spaces, and the headings show which files sit in each.
- **Contract:** the section no longer repeats what a contract is.
- **Folder tree:** it includes `.claude/hooks/save-transcript.sh`, because Traceability names it. The table still leaves it out, since who owns `.claude/` is undecided.

   - **Deep module**: the Contract section relies on it, and nothing explains it.
   - **Requirement**, **Steering** and **Implementation**: generic definitions, like Contract. I'd then trim their sections the same way.

repository when they contribute to it, and that it doesn't
cover how humans work with agents._

## Glossary

- **Solution space**: _How what's needed is met._

  never edits it._

  steering bullet and says whether the implementation can
  depart from it. There are five:_
  - **`ALWAYS`**: _A rule about what the implementation always
    does. No departure._
  - **`NEVER`**: _A rule about what the implementation never
    does. No departure._
  - **`FAVOR`**: _A preference for something. The
    implementation can depart from it, with a stated reason._
  - **`DISFAVOR`**: _A preference against something. The
    implementation can depart from it, with a stated reason._
  - **`CONSIDER`**: _Inspiration, not a preference. The
    implementation can ignore it without giving a reason._

_A folder tree of the fixed files this file names:
`README.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, `CLAUDE.md`,

root, and `.claude/hooks/save-transcript.sh`. Nothing the
implementation adds appears in it, so it never needs
updating as the implementation grows._

_A table of the major files and the implementation: what
each is for, and its ownership. `README.md`,

ownership. `REQUIREMENTS.md` is human-owned at its top

# Contributing

## Purpose of this file

_States that this file tells agents how to interact with this
repository when they contribute to it, and that it doesn't
cover how humans work with agents._

## Glossary

_One sentence: these terms are this repository's ubiquitous
language, in the domain-driven design sense, so they're used
with exactly these meanings everywhere._

- **Problem space**: _What's needed, independent of how it's
  met._
- **Solution space**: _How what's needed is met._
- **Requirement**: _A statement of something that's needed._
- **Contract**: _The interface through which the solution is
  used, saying nothing about how it's built._
- **Deep module**: _A module whose small, simple interface
  hides a large implementation._
- **Steering**: _Guidance on how the solution is built._
- **Steering keyword**: _The all-caps word that starts each
  steering bullet and says whether the implementation can
  depart from it. There are five:_
  - **`ALWAYS`**: _A rule about what the implementation always
    does. No departure._
  - **`NEVER`**: _A rule about what the implementation never
    does. No departure._
  - **`FAVOR`**: _A preference for something. The
    implementation can depart from it, with a stated reason._
  - **`DISFAVOR`**: _A preference against something. The
    implementation can depart from it, with a stated reason._
  - **`CONSIDER`**: _Inspiration, not a preference. The
    implementation can ignore it without giving a reason._
- **Implementation**: _The solution as built._
- **Human-owned**: _Comes entirely from the human._
- **Shared ownership**: _Created collaboratively by the human
  and agents. The human decides what goes in and understands
  all of it, so that comprehension debt is avoided._
- **Comprehension debt**: _The growing gap between how much
  content exists and how much of it is understood._
- **Agent-owned**: _Created entirely by the agent. The human
  isn't expected to understand all of it, or any of it, and
  never edits it._

## File layout and ownership

_A sentence on what the tree holds: only the files and
folders this file names that stay fixed as the
implementation grows, so nothing the implementation adds
goes in it. Then the tree: `README.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`,
`CLAUDE.md`, `REQUIREMENTS.md`, `CONTRACT.md` and
`STEERING.md` at the root, and
`.claude/hooks/save-transcript.sh`._

_A table of the major files and the implementation: what
each is for, and its ownership. `README.md`,
`CONTRIBUTING.md`, `CLAUDE.md` and `CONTRACT.md` have shared
ownership. `REQUIREMENTS.md` is human-owned at its top
level, with shared ownership below. `STEERING.md` is
human-owned. The implementation is agent-owned; its row
names no files or technology, and doesn't call it "every
other file"._

## Diagram

_A Mermaid diagram of the files and how they relate, laid
out with ELK. It shows `README.md` and `CLAUDE.md` leading
here, this file setting the rules, the requirements tree,
the contract on the boundary, the steering keywords and how
binding each is, and the implementation, each in its space.
Each arrow is labeled with its relationship, and colors show
the three kinds of ownership, with a legend. Renders on
GitHub._

## The two spaces

_The split between the problem space and the solution space
is strict: requirements never specify or prescribe the
solution's tech stack, and steering never states a need. The
contract sits on the boundary between them._

## Problem space files

### Requirements (`REQUIREMENTS.md`)

_Holds the requirements, as a tree. The top level comes
entirely from the human. Every other requirement is derived
from the one above it and cites that parent's ID, so every
line traces back to the top. The human derives the lower
levels, with an agent's help if wanted, and decides what
goes in and understands every line. A requirement is broken
down only when it needs more detail: the levels aren't the
same content restated, and no bottom level captures
everything._

## Boundary files

### Contract (`CONTRACT.md`)

_Holds the contract: narrow, following the deep modules
principle, and derived from the requirements as a whole, at
every level. Agreed like a requirement._

## Solution space files

### Steering (`STEERING.md`)

_Holds the steering, written by the human. It's a bullet
list in which every bullet starts with a steering keyword:
`ALWAYS`, `NEVER`, `FAVOR`, `DISFAVOR` or `CONSIDER`. It
covers only what sits behind the contract, so it can't
contradict the contract._

#### Conflicts

_Why steering can't directly contradict a requirement, and
what a seeming contradiction means: something is in the
wrong file. `ALWAYS` and `NEVER` rules can still rule out
every implementation that meets the requirements._

### Implementation

_Agent-owned. It implements the contract and meets every
requirement, at every level. The agent chooses the approach
and technology from the requirements, the contract and the
steering; the human shapes it only through those three
files._

## Analogies

_One line: the analogies below are explicitly unrelated to
this repository and give no direction for it._

### A Python library

_The analogy applied to the whole structure, part by part.
The contract is the library's `.pyi` stub files: the public
signatures, and nothing about how they're implemented._

### A web service with an HTTP API

_The analogy applied to the whole structure, part by part.
The contract is the service's OpenAPI spec._

### A mobile app

_The analogy applied to the whole structure, part by part.
The contract is the screens and actions its users see._

## Traceability

_The overarching rule that every change to this repository
is traceable, through the audit trails below._

### Commits, issues and agent transcripts

_All work starts from an issue. Every commit message links
that issue and the transcript of the agent session that
made the commit. Every issue links the transcripts of the
sessions that drafted or changed it. Transcripts live on the
`agent-transcripts` branch, one file per session, which
`.claude/hooks/save-transcript.sh` updates after every
turn._
